extracted.intended_audience: editors, referees, and researchers interested in scholarly peer review practices—especially in pure mathematics and science & technology studies
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and evaluation norms for peer reviewing pure-mathematics manuscripts, with emphasis on the 'quick opinion' (importance-only) stage used by top journals and its relation to full technical refereeing and editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two key judgments in peer review: correctness (soundness) and significance (importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review involves two central evaluations: (1) checking soundness/correctness (making sure the research is conducted correctly and proofs/results are valid), and (2) judging significance/importance (whether the results are sufficiently interesting/novel to be worth publishing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is foundational throughout the article; some journals emphasize soundness (e.g., PLOS ONE's 'soundness only' model) while others, especially top mathematics journals, focus first on significance. Editors and referees should be explicit which judgment they are being asked to make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick opinions (importance-only / executive / informal opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'quick opinion' is an expert judgment about a paper’s importance/significance that explicitly assumes the proofs are correct; it does not require checking correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'executive report' or 'first impression'. Editors solicit quick opinions to decide whether to send a paper for full technical refereeing. Solicitations often state: 'I am not asking for a full referee report, but only for your judgement of the importance of the results in the paper, so we can decide whether to get a full referee report.' Quick opinions are informal, brief, and addressed to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness-only review (mega-journal model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model of peer review where reviewers assess only the validity/soundness of the research and explicitly refrain from judging significance, deferring importance to post-publication attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: PLOS ONE. Serves as contrast to quick-opinion importance-only model. Use when journal policy aims to 'publish, then filter' rather than 'filter, then publish.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage reviewing process (split evaluation workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing workflow that first solicits quick opinions about importance from senior experts, and only after a positive quick opinion sends the paper to a technical referee to check correctness (technical/full report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a response to growing submission volumes and the time-consuming nature of checking correctness in mathematics. The two stages are: (a) quick opinion for significance, (b) detailed technical report for correctness and formal revision suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection by role and seniority
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors typically ask senior, well-known experts for quick opinions on importance and invite more junior but competent mathematicians to perform the time-consuming technical/full reports checking correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: senior scholars are seen as too busy for detailed checking; juniors often have time and benefit professionally from detailed refereeing. This division also helps expand the referee pool and can counteract 'ghost refereeing' by being explicit about who does the technical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick opinion reading/production expectations (speed and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick-opinion givers are expected to form judgments rapidly (often spending 'one to five minutes' or a brief skim), typically by reading the introduction and skimming the rest rather than verifying proofs in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors assume quick-opinion givers may already be familiar with the material (conference exposure, arXiv) and can 'sniff' or 'smell good' the paper. If an expert spends more time (e.g., half an hour), they may obtain a substantially better sense of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informality, tone, and audience of quick opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick opinions are written in an informal/colloquial style, often addressed to the editor rather than the author, sometimes not fully anonymous, and may include candid, gossipy, or frank remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I’ve seen nothing like this before!' or 'this kid' phrasing. Because they are often semi-private, quick opinions may reveal familiarity between referee and editor. Negative quick opinions are typically seen only by handling editors; there is ambiguity about whether the entire editorial board has access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of journal hierarchy as evaluative shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts and editors commonly name a journal to indicate the assessed 'level' or 'fit' of a paper (e.g., 'this is at <Journal-B> level, not <Journal-A>'), trading on a shared hierarchy of journals as a members’ measurement system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick opinions frequently characterize papers by comparing them to well-known journals; this is a common, socially understood shorthand for communicating significance. Mathematicians emphasize status/hierarchy rather than impact factor metrics when using this shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection practice by editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling editors often perform 'desk rejects'—rejecting 'complete rubbish' or 'clearly unsuitable' submissions themselves without external review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors do this frequently (e.g., 70–80% by decision), others rarely. Desk rejection is distinct from quick opinions: desk rejects are editorial triage, while quick opinions are solicited from external experts for borderline/significant submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick opinions as a source of referee suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors solicit quick opinions not only for judgments of importance but also to obtain names of suitable technical referees for the full report stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick-opinion givers often recommend trustworthy younger experts who could perform the detailed checking; this expands the editor’s pool and leverages senior experts' knowledge of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating a paper’s level as fixed (limited expectation of significance change after review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick opinions assume the paper’s significance is evident from its current form (introduction/main theorem) and treat the paper's level as relatively fixed rather than malleable through revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: papers are sometimes accepted 'as is' at other journals based on existing reports; peer review in mathematics is seen primarily to improve exposition and correctness, not to change core significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascading reports and inter-journal acceptance based on prior reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may forward reports or suggest submission to another journal, allowing other journals to use previously solicited quick/technical reports (cascading reports) and sometimes accept a paper 'as is' based on those reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an editor of multiple journals may accept a previously-rejected paper without further review; authors may be asked to have the next editor contact the prior editor to obtain referees’ identities and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-board decision-making informed by quick opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: At many top journals decisions are made by an editorial board; quick opinions serve as important 'data points' for board members when voting/deciding on acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At such journals, the content and the names of quick-opinion givers may be made available to the board; ambiguity exists about transparency to authors and to what extent the board reads quick opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of superficiality: missing important but hidden results
rubrics_metrics.description: A key criticism of quick opinions is that rapid, superficial reads can miss important contributions that are not obvious on a quick skim or are hidden in technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors worry that very technical work may require in-depth reading to reveal its importance; quick rejections may thus wrongly filter out significant but non-obvious results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of scholarly media in mathematics: dissemination vs validation/filtration/designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians split functions across media: preprint servers (e.g., arXiv) handle dissemination and registration, while traditional journals handle validation (checking correctness imperfectly), filtration, and—crucially—designation (career-signalling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlay journals evaluate arXiv papers and issue 'publications' consisting of certification/links and editorial introductions. Preprints accelerate dissemination, but journal publication remains important for designation and career credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in acceptance probability after positive quick opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive quick opinion affects but does not guarantee acceptance; in some journals a positive quick opinion implies an 80–90% chance of acceptance if the paper is shown to be correct, whereas in other journals acceptance after quick opinion remains below 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors described two groups of journals: ones that 'pre-accept' on positive quick opinions and others where technical referees still reassess significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to assume correctness when assessing importance
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for a quick opinion, reviewers are explicitly asked to assume that proofs are correct and to judge the paper's fit/importance on that basis (e.g., 'assuming that all the proofs are correct and clearly written...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicitations often restate this assumption to make clear the narrow scope of the quick opinion; this separates normative judgments about significance from technical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and confidentiality norms about quick opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is deliberate ambiguity and variability about who sees quick opinions (handling editor only vs entire editorial board), and about whether the content or identities are relayed to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors assume the entire board has access; others do not inform quick-opinion givers of the wider audience. Editors sometimes 'suitably edit' quick opinions before sharing with authors and often have little substantive content to pass on.
